newsitem.title: GERMANY: German government seeks cuts, tax estimates expected.
newsitem.headline: German government seeks cuts, tax estimates expected.

text.p: Chancellor Helmut Kohl called in ministers on Friday morning to discuss how to close a gap in German finances next year, with tax revenue estimates due out later likely to show a shortfall of billions of marks.

Finance Minister Theo Waigel wants spending cuts of three billion marks ($1.99 billion) including one billion from the Federal Labour Office, to finalise a 1997 budget by the start of next week which would meet entry terms for European Monetary Union.
Half-yearly tax revenue estimates were likely to be announced around midday (1100 GMT) after a two-day meeting of a working group in Erfurt.
Analysts expect federal inflows to be between two and three billion marks short of target, while tax revenues in Germany's 16 states could also be billions of marks below expectations.

Although the three-party governing coalition has set aside internal feuding over tax plans, Waigel is still under immense pressure to produce a budget that meets the Maastricht treaty's deficit target of three percent of gross domestic product.
"Bonn's financial chaos has become legendary. The tax estimates will hardly help it to touch up its worn-out image," the Handelsblatt newspaper said on Friday.

Unemployment has risen to post-unification highs, according to latest data published for October, but Waigel still wants cuts in federal transfers to cover the underfunded German unemployment insurance system next year.
His 1996 borrowing plans were blown away when he had to pay a 13 billion mark bailout to the Federal Labour Office, something he does not want to repeat.
But Labour Office chief Bernhard Jagoda says he needs 9.5 billion marks in extra federal transfers next year. Coalition members want to keep that figure down to four billion marks, Handelsblatt said.
